metadata.title: The Boondoggle Score: Label Who Does Each Step
metadata.description_blurb: Gru turns a build plan into a Boondoggle Score: each step names whether Claude acts, the human decides, or Claude drafts under review, with explicit handoff conditions before work proceeds.

beats.narration_text: He ran the /boondoggle command before starting his build. The Score table appeared: five steps, a labor column for each. He filled it in quickly — Claude-only on every row. His instructor asked him to read it back out loud. Step three: select the statistical method. Step five: set the classification threshold. He had written Claude-only for both. She asked: 'Do you know what method Claude will pick? Do you know if the threshold is right for this data?' He did not. This is Liam, in for Bear.

Gru is the software design document consultant behind the command. Not a code generator first — an architecture coach. Gru asks what you are proposing to build, what need it serves, what decisions are still unmade, and where Claude needs human review before the next step is allowed to happen.

items.label: Name the thing
items.sub: What are you actually proposing to build?

items.label: Set handoffs
items.sub: Claude can proceed only when “done” is explicit.

beats.new_visual_element: FormBCard — Gru as software design document consultant and handoff coach

beats.narration_text: Boondoggling is programming as conducting. Claude is very good at execution: scaffolding, syntax, transformations, drafts. The human still conducts: problem formulation, plausibility auditing, tool orchestration, interpretive judgment, and executive integration. The point is not to type less. The point is to decide more precisely.

items.label: Better handoffs
items.sub: Every step says who acts and what proves it is done.

beats.narration_text: That is what the Boondoggle Score makes visible. It is a table for each build step: what phase is this, who should do it, why that labor assignment is honest, and what condition must be true before the next step starts. Now the anatomy matters, because the Score is where vague confidence gets turned into accountable sequence.

items.label: Step and phase
items.sub: Where this action belongs in the build.

items.label: Handoff condition
items.sub: The explicit proof that the next step may begin.

beats.new_visual_element: FormBCard — Boondoggle Score purpose before anatomy

beats.narration_text: The Score table has five columns: step, phase, who does it, why, handoff condition. The who column has three values: Claude-only, human-only, and Claude-with-review. Claude-only means the step is purely mechanical and the outcome is verifiable. Human-only means the decision requires domain judgment that Claude cannot supply. Claude-with-review means Claude drafts, human checks before anything proceeds.

items.label: Human-only
items.sub: Decision needs domain judgment Claude cannot supply.

items.label: Claude-with-review
items.sub: Claude drafts, human checks before proceeding.

beats.new_visual_element: FormBCard — three values in the who column (Claude-only / Human-only / Claude-with-review)

beats.narration_text: Brooks 1986 distinguished essential from accidental complexity. Accidental: the friction of building — syntax errors, boilerplate, scaffolding. Essential: deciding what to build, choosing the method, setting the threshold. Claude eats accidental complexity. Essential complexity belongs to the human. When you write Claude-only for a step that requires domain judgment, you have handed over the essential work and kept the accidental.

items.label: Accidental
items.sub: Syntax errors, boilerplate, scaffolding — Claude eats this.

items.label: Essential
items.sub: What to build, which method, which threshold — the human's.

beats.narration_text: A Score where every row says Claude-only is a signal: either the build is trivial, or you have quietly handed over the human work and cannot yet see it. The Score cannot lie — you can write a vague build description, but you cannot write a vague handoff condition without hearing the vagueness. 'Claude decides' is not a handoff condition. 'Classification threshold verified against baseline dataset' is.
beats.new_visual_element: FormBCard — vague vs specific handoff condition (Popper move)

beats.narration_text: The Score is not a judgment about capability — Claude is capable of many things. It is a prompt for your own judgment: which steps require a decision that only you can make? The Score forces that question before any code runs. A build with two human-only rows and three Claude-only rows is an honest build. A build with zero human-only rows is probably not.

artifactLines: Not a capability judgment — a prompt for yours.
Forces the who-decides question before code runs.
Zero human-only rows: probably not honest.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this: you want to understand the Boondoggle Score anatomy before applying it. Ask Claude to walk you through each column — what it measures, what a red flag looks like in that column, and what a score above eight means for the build.

props.command: Walk me through the anatomy of the Boondoggle Score: what does each column measure, what does a red flag look like in each column, and what does a total score above eight mean for whether I should proceed with this build plan?
props.runningText: paste your spec, CLAUDE.md, or build plan here…

beats.narration_text: If this surfaces the human-only step you almost gave to Claude, subscribe. Liam, in for Bear.
